title: Oracle and Quantinuum Partner to Deploy Quantum Computing on the Cloud
excerpt: The multi-year deal will place Quantinuum's Helios quantum computer inside an Oracle AI data center, marking an industry first for on-site quantum-classical integration.
body:
• Oracle Cloud Infrastructure customers will gain access to Quantinuum's Helios quantum computer through a multi-year partnership
  • Helios will be deployed in a U.S.-based Oracle AI data center, marking an industry first for on-site quantum-classical colocation
  • The deal comes alongside Quantinuum's first post-IPO earnings report, with revenue up 279% to $8 million
  • Oracle plans to preview its quantum computing service in the coming months

Oracle and Quantinuum announced a multi-year partnership on Tuesday aimed at bringing quantum computing capabilities to Oracle's cloud platform, as major technology firms race to commercialize the nascent technology.

Under the deal, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure customers will gain access to Quantinuum's Helios quantum computer through OCI's quantum service, allowing them to combine quantum computing with Oracle's graphics-processing and high-performance computing services. Financial terms and a deployment date were not disclosed.

An Industry First

The partnership marks a significant milestone for the quantum computing industry. Quantinuum's Helios system, which was commercially launched in November, will be deployed in a U.S.-based Oracle AI data center — making it the first time a quantum computer has been colocated within a major cloud provider's own facility for direct customer use.

https://x.com/StockSavvyShay/status/2087268168926650727

While Quantinuum has historically offered its quantum systems through third-party cloud platforms including Amazon Braket and Microsoft Azure Quantum, the Oracle deal represents a shift toward deeper infrastructure integration. Running on-site within OCI, Helios is expected to work with existing Oracle services under the same governance and security frameworks that enterprise customers already use.

"We believe the next phase of enterprise computing will be shaped by bringing quantum, AI and high-performance computing together."

— Rajeeb Hazra, CEO, Quantinuum

Hazra said the partnership would "create a unique deeply integrated environment for hybrid workloads." Oracle plans to preview its quantum service in the coming months, combining Quantinuum's development stack with open-source hybrid-programming frameworks to help developers build and test quantum-classical applications.

Post-IPO Momentum

The announcement came alongside Quantinuum's first earnings report since its initial public offering in June, in which the company raised $1.68 billion in an upsized offering. The results beat Wall Street expectations.

Quantinuum reported a loss of 28 cents per share on revenue of $8 million for the second quarter, compared with analyst estimates of a 28-cent loss on $7.6 million in revenue. Revenue surged 279% year-over-year from a modest base, reflecting the company's early-stage commercialization trajectory.

The Oracle system sale pushed management to raise its full-year bookings forecast to at least $120 million, up from $81 million as of the end of June. Quantinuum also guided full-year revenue to $30 million at the midpoint, above consensus estimates of $26.5 million.

"This was a good first quarter post-IPO," Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore said in a note. "Bookings are tracking better, there is revenue upside both this year and next, which suggests both conservatism in the original outlook and incremental commercial activity."

Market Validation

Quantinuum stock rose about 5% on the news. Jefferies analyst Kevin Garrigan said the Oracle partnership "reinforces Quantinuum's position at the center of emerging AI-quantum infrastructure." The company ended the quarter with over $2 billion in cash on its balance sheet, providing a substantial runway for R&D and manufacturing scale-up.

The companies said they plan to explore how hybrid quantum-AI infrastructure could address computationally intensive challenges facing enterprises, while also broadening access for universities and research institutions advancing scientific discovery.

What's Next

The deal positions Oracle as a late but serious entrant into the quantum computing cloud space, joining AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and IBM, all of which have offered some form of quantum access for years. For Quantinuum, it extends the company's reach into one of the largest enterprise infrastructure ecosystems in the world.

The quantum computing sector has attracted growing investor and enterprise attention this year, buoyed by a federal funding package that broadly lifted the sector and a wave of public listings including Xanadu Quantum Technologies and Quantinuum itself.
